citations.quote: Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. If $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and fix $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. For a vector Fourier coefficient $a(k)\in\mathbb C^d$, define $(Pa)(k)=P_ka(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, where $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k
e0$. For a tensor field $F=(F_{ij})_{i,j=1}^d$ with coefficients in any $H^s(Q_d)$, define the scalar pressure map $Q$ by $\widehat{QF}(0)=0$ and $\widehat{QF}(k)=-\sum_{i,j=1}^d k_i k_j|k|^{-2}\widehat F_{ij}(k)$ for $k
e0$. For $q\in H^s(Q_d)$, define $\partial_jq\in H^{s-1}(Q_d)$ coefficientwise by $\widehat{\partial_jq}(k)=ik_j\widehat q(k)$; for vector fields set $\widehat{
abla q}(k)=ik\widehat q(k)$, and for tensor fields set $\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}_i(k)=i\sum_jk_j\widehat F_{ij}(k)$. These derivative maps are bounded from $H^s$ to $H^{s-1}$. The multipliers $P$ and $Q$ are real-preserving and bounded on every $H^s$, $s\in\mathbb R$; $P$ is an orthogonal projection and commutes with these derivatives. For every $F$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, their exact identity is the coefficientwise equality
$$\widehat{
abla QF}(k)=-(I-P_k)\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k).$$
In particular, both sides have zero coefficient at $k=0$.

derivations.claim: The smoothness assumptions make $v\otimes v$, $\partial_t v$, $\Delta v$, and $f$ well-defined periodic fields. By [F1] these fields lie in the required $L^2$ spaces. The adopted projector convention is conditional on the explicit Countable Choice premise [F2], and [F3] defines the multiplier on each term; hence the displayed formula defines $r_v$ at every $t\in[0,T]$.

The maps $t\mapsto \partial_t v$, $t\mapsto\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v)$, $t\mapsto\Delta v$, and $t\mapsto f$ are continuous into $L^2$; boundedness of $P$ from [F3] preserves that continuity. Hence $r_v\in C([0,T];L^2)$, and compactness of $[0,T]$ gives $\int_0^T\|r_v(t)\|_2dt<\infty$. Also $v(0)-u_0\in L^2$, so $d_0$ is finite.

This is an actual public definitional biconditional, not inherited supplier context: the Definition explicitly says smooth spatial w is solenoidal/divergence-free iff div w(x)=0 for every x, and smooth time-dependent w is solenoidal iff div w(t,x)=0 for every(t,x). Forward direction unfolds the adopted predicates: a solenoidal u0 has sum_j partial_j(u0)_j(x)=0 on Q_d, and a solenoidal v has sum_j partial_j v_j(t,x)=0 on[0,T]xQ_d. The preceding componentwise divergence definitions fix those expressions and specify spatial derivatives only. Current Facts Given records exactly div v=div u0=0; proof1.1 assumes these defined smooth fields when forming the residual. This is definition elimination, not a PDE-existence, distributional or Fourier-projection equivalence.

case_scope.source_excerpt: A smooth spatial field $w:Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$ is solenoidal, or divergence-free, iff $\operatorname{div}w(x)=0$ for every $x\in Q_d$; a smooth time-dependent field $w:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$ is solenoidal iff $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)=0$ for every $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times Q_d$.

boundaries.evidence: For either stated smooth map class, if the displayed componentwise spatial divergence vanishes at every point of its domain, then the map satisfies precisely the defining predicate solenoidal (and, in the spatial clause, its synonymous name divergence-free). Thus pointwise divergence-zero u0 and v qualify as the solenoidal reference/approximation fields in the residual Definition. Current Facts Given uses those same conditions; proof1.1–2.1 then establishes residual well-definedness, continuity and finite time-integrated L2 norm. No independent theorem is required for this definition introduction, and no implication from Pf=f, a weak derivative condition or zero residual to solenoidality is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized volume $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For a vector field $w$, use the componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat w(k)=\int_{Q_d}w(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$ and norm $\|w\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|w(x)|^2\,d\mu(x))^{1/2}$. Define $P_0=I$ and, for $k\ne0$, $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$, with $\widehat{Pw}(k)=P_k\widehat w(k)$; $P$ is the Leray projector. For a smooth spatial vector field $w:Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$, define $\operatorname{div}w(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jw_j(x)$; for a smooth time-dependent vector field $w:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$, define $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jw_j(t,x)$, with derivatives taken only in $x$; for a tensor field $F=(F_{ij})$, set $(\operatorname{div}F)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_{ij}$, and set $(v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_i v_j$. Let $\Delta=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2$. A smooth spatial field $w:Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$ is solenoidal, or divergence-free, iff $\operatorname{div}w(x)=0$ for every $x\in Q_d$; a smooth time-dependent field $w:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$ is solenoidal iff $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)=0$ for every $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times Q_d$. Given a constant $\nu\ge0$, smooth $f:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$, a smooth solenoidal field $v:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$, and a smooth solenoidal reference initial field $u_0:Q_d\to\mathbb R^d$, define the continuous residual and initial defect by

$$r_v:=\partial_t v+P\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v)-\nu\Delta v-Pf,\qquad d_0:=\|v(0,\cdot)-u_0\|_2.$$

The residual is a continuous function of time with values in $L^2(Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$, so $\int_0^T\|r_v(t,\cdot)\|_2\,dt$ is finite. This is a continuous-domain residual: finitely many collocation values do not by themselves bound this $L^1_tL^2_x$ quantity. All quantities here are mathematical; no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

For every $F$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, their exact identity is the coefficientwise equality
$$\widehat{
abla QF}(k)=-(I-P_k)\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k).$$
In particular, both sides have zero coefficient at $k=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim:
Set $e=v-u$. Under the explicit Countable Choice convention [F4], subtracting the exact equation from the residual equation [F1] gives $\partial_te+P\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v-u\otimes u)-
u\Delta e=r_v$. Since $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{div}v=0$, the tensor convention gives $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes v)=v\cdot
abla v$ and $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)=u\cdot
abla u$; the difference is $v\cdot
abla e+e\cdot
abla u$.

Pair the resulting equation with $e$ in normalized $L^2$. By [F2], $Pe=e$ and $P$ is self-adjoint, so each projected transport term paired with $e$ equals its unprojected pairing. Periodicity gives $\int_{Q_d}\operatorname{div}(v|e|^2)\,d\mu=0$; since $\operatorname{div}v=0$, this yields $\langle v\cdot
abla e,eangle= rac12\int v\cdot
abla|e|^2\,d\mu=0$. Also $|\langle e\cdot
abla u,eangle|\le\sup_x\|
abla u\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|e\|_2^2$. Periodic integration by parts gives $\langle-
u\Delta e,eangle=
u\|
abla e\|_2^2\ge0$. By [F3], $|\langle r_v,eangle|\le\|r_v\|_2\|e\|_2$. Using $\langle\partial_t e,eangle= rac12 rac{d}{dt}\|e\|_2^2$ now gives $ rac12 rac{d}{dt}\|e\|_2^2\le \sup_x\|
abla u\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|e\|_2^2+\|r_v\|_2\|e\|_2$.

For $\delta>0$ put $y_\delta(t)=(\|e(t)\|_2^2+\delta^2)^{1/2}$ and $a(t)=\sup_x\|\nabla u(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Continuity of $\nabla u$ on compact $[0,T]\times Q_d$ makes $a$ continuous, so the definition of $A$ gives $A'(t)=a(t)$. The differential inequality in step 2.1 and the bounds $\|e\|_2^2/y_\delta\le y_\delta$ and $\|e\|_2/y_\delta\le1$ imply $y_\delta'(t)\le A'(t)y_\delta(t)+\|r_v(t)\|_2$.

The product rule and $A'(t)=\sup_x\|\nabla u(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ show that $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-A(t)}y_\delta(t))\le e^{-A(t)}\|r_v(t)\|_2$. Integrating from $0$ to $t$ and multiplying by $e^{A(t)}$ gives $y_\delta(t)\le e^{A(t)}y_\delta(0)+\int_0^t e^{A(t)-A(s)}\|r_v(s)\|_2ds$. As $\delta\downarrow0$, $y_\delta(t)\to\|e(t)\|_2$ and $y_\delta(0)\to\|v(0)-u_0\|_2$, which proves the stated estimate.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a specified probability space of inputs, let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty common time interval, and let $(X,\mathcal X)$ be a specified measurable state or path space. An exact selected solution map is a supplied measurable map $S:\Theta\to X$ whose values solve the specified mathematical model on $I$. The equation, solution class and admissible input set are supplied as data; a smooth uniqueness theorem may identify a single-valued map, but measurability is a separate required hypothesis. In a nonunique weak theory an actual measurable selection must be given before taking a pushforward law; this definition asserts no selection theorem. More generally a supplied measurable random state is allowed without any PDE interpretation. A real observable is a map $J:X\to\mathbb R$ such that $Y:=J\circ S$ is measurable. It is integrable or square-integrable when $\mathbb E_\mu|Y|<\infty$ or $\mathbb E_\mu Y^2<\infty$, respectively.

For a nonempty set $H$ of numerical settings, supplied measurable numerical composites $Y_h=J_h\circ S_h$ define approximate outputs on the same input law; the maps $S_h$ may take values in specified approximation spaces $X_h$, with $J_h:X_h\to\mathbb R$. When $Y,Y_h$ are integrable, define $\theta=\mathbb E_\mu Y$, $\theta_h=\mathbb E_\mu Y_h$ and signed mean bias $b_h=\theta_h-\theta$. Output variances require finite second moments. This definition implies neither IID sampling nor numerical convergence, a bias bound, or physical applicability. All exact and approximate outputs must use the same declared scalar unit before forming their bias.

The finite-second-moment spatial velocity law and sensor are included as follows. Let $H_D=L^2(D,\mathcal D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ and let $\mu_H$ be the supplied finite-second-moment probability law on $(H_D,\mathcal B(H_D))$. Take $\Theta=X=H_D$, $\mathcal A=\mathcal X=\mathcal B(H_D)$, $\mu=\mu_H$, $S=\operatorname{id}_{H_D}$, and $J=S_\psi$ for the supplied weight $\psi\in H_D$. Thus the input itself is the random velocity class and $Y(v)=S_\psi(v)$. The identity map is measurable, and the pairing lemma gives measurability and a finite second moment under exactly $\mu_H$. This use is on quotient classes and requires no measurable choice of pointwise representatives. In the general separable Banach-state branch, bounded linear sensors have the same measurability and moment property by their operator bounds. Time-series sampling, a Markov chain, and mixing remain additional assumptions; dependent consecutive readings are not IID merely because this definition applies.

The earlier pointwise-field formulation is also included: let $d_s\in\{2,3\}$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_s}$ be nonempty and Lebesgue-measurable, and let $(\mathscr V,\mathcal V)$ be any specified measurable space of product-measurable fields $u:D\times I\to\mathbb R^{d_s}$. Use $X=\mathscr V$, a supplied measurable random-field map, and measurable scalar composites. Passing from an $L^2$ class to such a pointwise random field requires a supplied jointly measurable representative; it is not part of the quotient-sensor specialization. Velocity components use one fixed velocity unit, and sensor weights carry the corresponding integral units.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

derivations.claim: The Lipschitz map $J$ is continuous, so the measurable state maps make $J\circ S$ and $J\circ\widetilde S$ measurable scalar observables as in [F1]. By [A2], $\int g^2d\mu\le C\int gd\mu=C$, hence $\|g\|_{L^2(\mu)}\le\sqrt C$. For every $z\in\mathcal Z$, $|J(S(z))|\le|J(0)|+L\|S(z)\|_X$; [F2] and [A1] therefore give $\int |J(S)|g\,d\mu\le |J(0)|+L\|\|S\|_X\|_{L^2(\mu)}\|g\|_{L^2(\mu)}<\infty$. The same estimate with $\widetilde S$ proves both target expectations are finite.

The target-density definition and Lipschitz condition give
$$\left|\mathbb E_\nu[J(S)]-\mathbb E_\nu[J(\widetilde S)]\right|=\left|\int (J(S)-J(\widetilde S))g\,d\mu\right|\le L\int\|S-\widetilde S\|_Xg\,d\mu.$$
The integral is well-defined by step 1.1 and $g\ge0$.
Apply [F2] to $\|S-\widetilde S\|_X$ and $g$, then use the mean-square bound in [A1] and $\|g\|_2\le\sqrt C$ from step 1.1. This bounds the last integral in step 2.1 by $\varepsilon\sqrt C$.
Multiplying the step 3.1 bound by $L$ in step 2.1 proves the claimed inequality.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes a probability measure mu, so the input space cannot be empty.
If ε=0, step 3.1 makes the last integral in step 2.1 zero; if L=0, step 2.1 gives zero bias directly. Step 4.1 concludes the stated bound in either case.
On a one-point input space μ=ν and g=1; steps 2.1–4.1 reduce to the pointwise Lipschitz estimate with the stated mean-square error.
If C=1, g=1 μ-a.e. because 0≤g≤1 and ∫g dμ=1; steps 2.1–4.1 then give the usual Lε estimate.

The proof fixes the displayed measures and maps and uses no choice principle.
The proposition gives an inequality, not a biconditional.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on it, meaning a countably additive measure on $\Sigma$ with $\mu(\mathcal Z)=1$. Let $X$ be a real normed vector space and give it the norm-Borel $\sigma$-algebra generated by its norm-open sets. Let $S,\widetilde S:\mathcal Z\to X$ be measurable maps. Let $J:X\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz, meaning $|J(x)-J(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_X$ for all $x,y\in X$, with $L\ge0$. Suppose

$$\int_{\mathcal Z}\bigl(\|S\|_X^2+\|\widetilde S\|_X^2\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,\qquad \int_{\mathcal Z}\|S-\widetilde S\|_X^2\,d\mu\le\varepsilon^2$$

for some finite $\varepsilon\ge0$. For a measurable scalar function $h$, write $\|h\|_{L^2(\mu)}=(\int_{\mathcal Z}|h|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$. Let $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $\int g\,d\mu=1$ and $g\le C$ $\mu$-almost everywhere for a finite $C\ge1$, and define the target probability law by $\nu(E)=\int_Eg\,d\mu$ for $E\in\Sigma$, with target expectation $\mathbb E_\nu[H]=\int Hg\,d\mu$ whenever the integral exists. Then the measurable scalar observables $J\circ S$ and $J\circ\widetilde S$ are $\nu$-integrable and

$$\left|\mathbb E_\nu[J(S)]-\mathbb E_\nu[J(\widetilde S)]\right|\le L\sqrt C\,\varepsilon.$$

The estimate assumes a population mean-square error under $\mu$ and a bounded target density $g$; a finite test sample by itself establishes neither assumption. The state space may represent fluid fields when that measurable state model is supplied. For a physical application, both observables must use the same declared scalar unit; this mathematical proposition assigns no physical units.

Under $\mu=\delta_0$, both $S(0)$ and $\widetilde S(0)$ equal zero, so $\mathbb E_\mu\|S-\widetilde S\|_X^2=0$; the separate state second moments are also finite because the maps have finite range.

Under $

The set $\{1\}$ has $\mu$-measure zero and $
u$-measure one. If a target density $g$ existed, then $
